story.script: For weeks, everyone stayed two unpaid hours late because he claimed head office had ordered it, and the rule finally cracked that night when I asked payroll which policy code belonged on our timesheets. He had repeated the same warning so often that most of us stopped questioning it. Every evening he stood near the door, watched the clock hit six, and reminded us that leaving on time would be remembered during performance reviews. I had been staying too, mostly because nobody wanted to be the first person to challenge him. Then he posted another message saying the overtime rule was non-negotiable. I replied politely and asked for the policy number so I could record the hours correctly. He told me not to overcomplicate things and insisted the instruction came directly from head office. I forwarded his message to payroll and asked which overtime code I should select. Twenty minutes later, payroll replied that there was no mandatory overtime policy, there was no special code, and any approved overtime had to be requested formally and paid. They copied HR. My manager stopped replying immediately. The next morning HR asked the entire team to send them every message about the supposed rule. By lunch, the pinned overtime announcement had disappeared and a new message said everyone should follow normal contracted hours unless overtime was officially approved. My manager called it a misunderstanding, but the email trail made that explanation difficult. Payroll then asked us to submit the extra hours we had already worked for review. I had only asked for one policy code, but that single question ended the fake rule and turned weeks of unpaid overtime into a problem my manager had to explain himself.
